0-4405-1-3.subevent: A double-decker bus overturned on the A385 between Totnes and Paignton while traveling from Torquay to Plymouth at about 11:00 BST, leaving dozens injured.
Police said up to eight people had been seriously hurt and were undergoing assessment.
A total of 37 people are being treated at several hospitals around Devon, according to the NHS.
The emergency services closed the road and a major incident was declared, which has now been stood down.
Uninjured passengers were taken to Paignton bus station for support and help to continue their journeys.

Jane Viner, chief nurse and deputy chief executive at Torbay and South Devon Foundation Trust, said many NHS staff had come in on their day off to help deal with the casualties and that it has been a huge team effort by emergency services and hospital staff.
Gerald Taylor, the area manager for Devon & Somerset Fire and Rescue Service, said the road will stay shut in both directions for several hours for investigation and recovery.
Police said the bus driver had not been arrested, confirming he was assisting them with their inquiries.
A witness said there were emergency vehicles everywhere.
A spokesman for Stagecoach South West said the company was helping emergency services and its thoughts were with the victims, and that safety is their priority and they will assist the investigation.
Several ambulances and the air ambulance were sent to the scene.
The Liberal Democrat MP for Totnes, Sarah Wollaston, thanked the emergency services for their efforts under difficult circumstances.

9-21073-2-1.subevent: The Portuguese Episcopal Conference announced on Jan. 21 that public Masses would be suspended in Portugal from Jan. 23.
The bishops cited the 'extreme gravity' of the coronavirus crisis as the reason for the suspension.
They stated that it is a moral imperative for all citizens, particularly Christians, to take maximum sanitary precautions.
Portugal recorded 609,000 COVID-19 cases and 9,920 deaths as of Jan. 22, reflecting a surge in deaths.
This is the second suspension of public worship by the bishops; the first occurred in March 2020 and was eased at the end of May.
The bishops announced that public Masses, catechesis, and other pastoral activities requiring gatherings would be suspended from Jan. 23.
They called on priests to offer livestreamed Masses.
Earlier in January, the bishops had called for the suspension or postponement of baptisms, confirmations, and marriages.
They said that funerals could be celebrated according to norms issued in May 2020, requiring social distancing.
A Lenten retreat for the bishops scheduled for Feb. 22-26 has been canceled.
The Shrine of Our Lady of Fatima announced it will broadcast three Masses and two rosary prayers daily while public Masses are suspended.
Shrine rector Fr. Carlos Cabecinhas said that following via television is not the same as physical presence but is the only possible way to participate now.

2-35077-7-1.subevent: Human Rights Watch survey finds lives of LGBTQ+ Afghans have dramatically worsened under Taliban rule.
The report recorded nearly 60 cases of targeted violence against LGBTQ+ people since August 2021.
Heather Barr said that before the Taliban takeover, people had hope for gradual improvement, but on 15 August 2021, all of that ended.
Homosexuality was banned under former president Ashraf Ghani, but the Taliban vowed to take a hard line against LGBT rights, citing sharia law.
J Lester Feder reported that LGBT Afghans have survived gang-rape, mob attacks, or been hunted by family members who joined the Taliban.
Zeba Gul described that her life worsened after the Taliban came to power, including family abuse before the takeover.
After the Taliban took power, Zeba Gul's family threw her out, and she was attacked, raped, and held and beaten by the Taliban for three days.
Faraydoon Fakoori stated that the situation for gender minorities in Afghanistan has worsened after the Taliban's arrival.
Zeba Gul said that the return of the Taliban empowered vigilantes and homophobes, with no fear of punishment.
A Taliban spokesperson told Bild newspaper that for homosexuals, the only punishments are stoning or standing behind a wall that will fall down on them.

9-21751-1-5.subevent: Clashes broke out Sunday morning in three cities across Israel as police attempted to enforce coronavirus lockdown restrictions in ultra-Orthodox communities.
In the Jerusalem neighborhood of Mea Shearim, hundreds of people clashed with police attempting to shut down a yeshiva that had opened illegally.
Police officers at the yeshiva were surrounded by a crowd shouting insults and throwing trash and debris, leading to one arrest and the use of water cannons to disperse the crowd.
In Ashdod, police were confronted while closing an ultra-Orthodox elementary school that had opened in violation of Health Ministry and Education Ministry rules.
Police said several dozen people tried to force their way into the school compound, injured four officers, damaged the fence, and four people were arrested.

In Bnei Brak, several clashes broke out as police tried to shut down schools linked to the Vizhnitz Hasidic dynasty, whose head rabbi initially ruled that schools should open before backtracking hours later.
Police stated they would continue to enforce virus restrictions in all communities.
The lockdown, in its third week and extended till January 31, shut all nonessential businesses and the entire education system except special education.

Last week, clashes broke out in Bnei Brak between police and rioters opposed to lockdown restrictions, with at least six arrests, and the rioters belonged to an extremist faction of the Vizhnitz Hasidic sect.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the Friday attack in Bnei Brak, stating that 'we will act with a heavy hand against lawbreakers.'
Critics accused Netanyahu of avoiding a crackdown on the Haredi public to not anger his ultra-Orthodox coalition partners.
Additional lockdown violations among the ultra-Orthodox emerged Saturday, including a mass gathering in the Sanz Hasidic sect in Netanya.
Health Minister Yuli Edelstein called for jailing those who broke lockdown rules.
Netanyahu and Edelstein appealed to Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky to influence the community; Kanievsky gave permission for some schools to reopen only if it does not spark confrontation with police.
Haredi communities have suffered disproportionately from the coronavirus due to high infection rates partly caused by rule-breaking.
The Health Ministry reported 2,394 new COVID-19 cases on Saturday, with total infections at 595,097, deaths at 4,361, and 1,228 patients in serious condition.

1-wiki-img/15489-4/15489-4-3.subevent: Researchers have narrowed down how Pluto's giant ice blades form.
The blades are made mostly of methane ice and form similarly to penitentes on Earth.
New Horizons flew by Pluto in July 2015 and observed varied terrains.
The jagged spikes form at the highest altitudes where methane freezes directly from gas to solid.
When the climate warms, parts of the methane ice sublimate back to gas.
Jeffrey Moore stated that climate variation causes the methane ice to evaporate.
On Earth, such structures are called penitentes and are much shorter.
Penitentes on Earth form due to sunlight concentrating on irregularities.
Pluto's penitentes provide information about surface and air temperature changes over time.
The link between methane and high elevations helps map Pluto's topography.
The new work will appear in the journal Icarus.

0-4766-1-3.subevent: A South West Aviation Let L-410, registration UR-TWO, with 20 passengers and 3 crew, impacted Yirol Lake near Yirol City while on approach.
Local fishermen recovered 19 bodies from the lake; 4 survivors were taken to a hospital with serious injuries.
On September 10, 2018, authorities reported that 20 people died and 3 passengers survived the accident.
The Information Minister in Eastern Lakes State reported the aircraft carried 23 people, with 19 bodies recovered and 4 survivors taken to hospital.
South Sudan's Civil Aviation Authority opened an investigation into the crash.
On September 9, 2018, The Aviation Herald received a passenger manifest listing South West Aviation as the operator and UR-TWO as the aircraft.
Russian databases updated information on the aircraft, showing it was previously operated by Universal-Avia and later owned by SlavAir, with tail number UR-TWO.
The aircraft was restored to flying condition in Rivne, Ukraine in 2016, with the operator name 'South West' and a South Sudanese phone number on the paint scheme.
Ukraine's Aircraft Registry assigned tail number UR-TWO to the L-410 on April 11, 2018, with owner SlavAir Company and no operator mentioned.
On November 19, 2018, Ukraine's NBAAI reported that SlavAir's L-410 UR-TWO crashed at Yirol, killing 20 and injuring 3, with SSCAA investigating.
Between October 29 and November 2, 2018, the NBAAI read out and decrypted parametric data from the aircraft.

On October 23, 2019, Ukraine's NBAAI published the final report from South Sudan's Ministry of Transport, concluding that probable causes included bad weather, pilot error in altimeter setting, and an unreported propeller replacement.
The SSMOT reported that the crew (captain and first officer) lost their logbooks and had not been inspected by South Sudan's Civil Aviation Authority.
The weather forecast for Yirol on the day of the accident indicated fog with visibility less than a few meters, and the crew circled several times before crash landing into Lake Yirol.
The FDR's photosensitive film had ended by the time of the accident, so no flight data was recorded.

The SSMOT released findings including that the aircraft was owned by SlavAir and leased to Southwest, the crew was different from those who ferried the aircraft, propeller maintenance was done without a release certificate, and no weather briefing was obtained.

5-wiki-img/5789-8/5789-8-2.subevent: A report says climate change can be tackled if people embrace major lifestyle shifts.
The authors compiled a list of top ways to reduce carbon footprint based on 7000 studies.
The report calls for re-ordering government priorities to protect the planet.
Living car-free is ranked first, saving 2.04 tonnes CO2 annually.
Driving electric cars and taking fewer long-haul flights are also top actions.
Switching to a vegan diet helps but less than transport; recycling is less effective.
Lead author Dr Diana Ivanova argues for a change of mindset and carbon limits.
She says the coronavirus lockdown shows many could live without cars.
She says rich people consume most and aviation is under-taxed.
Other top actions include renewable power, public transport, home insulation, heat pumps, and improved cookstoves.
The study says implementing measures would save about nine tonnes CO2 per person per year.
Experts note the study is valuable but only considers carbon footprint, not other impacts.

19-28321-12-t.subevent: Muslims accept that the death penalty is a punishment established by God in the Qur'an, which teaches that capital punishment is acceptable when required by law.
The Prophet Muhammad sentenced people to death for murder.
Shari'ah law states that the punishment for murder, adultery, and denying Islam is the death penalty.
Some Muslims argue that although capital punishment is allowed in the Qur'an, it is not compulsory.
Shari'ah law allows the family of a murder victim to accept money as reparation rather than enforce the death penalty.
Some Muslims believe that only Allah has the right to take life, and carrying out the death penalty is 'playing God' and committing shirk.

1-14826-2-3.subevent: Alicia Soto attended the 1 October Sunrise Remembrance Ceremony for the third consecutive year.
Soto said attending the ceremony has helped her process her trauma from the Route 91 Harvest music festival mass shooting.
Soto moved from California to Minneapolis and became a flight attendant, deciding to live life to the fullest for those who died.
A slideshow displayed the names and pictures of the 58 people killed that night, plus the pictures of two women who died within the past year.
Clark County Sheriff Joe Lombardo announced that Kimberly Gervais and Samanta Arjune will be added to the official death toll, raising it to 60.
The announcement followed a Review-Journal article that reported the police department's initial decision not to include them.
Lombardo said he is comfortable acknowledging that the two women lost their lives as a result of October 1.
The ceremony had fewer attendees due to the coronavirus pandemic, forcing officials to limit attendance.
Gov. Steve Sisolak said that raising the limit on public gatherings made Thursday's event one of his biggest priorities.
Sisolak offered condolences to the families and said they will never forget what happened.
Albert Rivera, father of victim Jordyn Rivera, thanked survivors for continuing to come together and support each other.
Rivera acknowledged Greg Zanis, who built crosses for the victims and died in May of terminal bladder cancer.
Rivera called for unity, urging people to remember how they came together on October 2, 2017.

1-15289-5-1.subevent: President Joko Widodo requested that the revision process of the Coal and Mineral Mining Law be suspended.
Incoming legislators began discussing the revisions despite Jokowi's request.
A working committee of House members and the government resumed deliberations on the revisions.
Students demanded outright rejection of the revisions and led mass protests across Indonesia.
On September 25, Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources officials submitted an unfinished list of 938 concerns to initiate deliberation.
The DPR abandoned its plans to push through the revisions after public pressure and the president's call.
The working committee convened and agreed on 235 of 703 proposed changes.
The draft under discussion remained unchanged from the previous year.
The proposed revisions would allow companies to extend permits without offering concessions to state-owned companies and remove prison terms for corrupt officials.
The revisions would remove companies' responsibility for rehabilitating mining sites, including filling pits, and add fines and prison terms for hindering mining activities.
The revisions removed communities' right to veto mining activities.

1-15091-1-1.subevent: In December 2020, a 110-million-year-old dinosaur named Ubirajara jubatus was described with unique features including furlike filaments and spearlike feathers.
The fossil sparked a legal and ethical controversy between German paleontologists and officials, who claim the fossil, and the Brazilian scientific community, which wants it back.
The journal Cretaceous Research retracted the paper describing Ubirajara jubatus.
Brazilian paleontologists questioned the legality of the fossil's export, citing a 1942 Brazilian law that requires permits for collecting fossils and a 1990 decree requiring export approval.
The original paper stated that the fossil was brought to Germany in 1995 with an export permit signed by a Brazilian official.
A German ministry spokesperson said the fossil was actually imported in 2006 by a private company and acquired by the State Museum of Natural History Karlsruhe in 2009.
Social media campaign #UbirajaraBelongstoBR accused the authors and museum of illegally taking the fossil.
The journal temporarily withdrew the paper on December 24, 2020, while the controversy played out.
The Baden-Württemberg ministry backed the museum's ownership claim, stating the fossil was legally acquired under German law.
The Brazilian paleontology community expressed outrage at the ministry's ownership claim.
Cretaceous Research permanently withdrew the paper, citing unresolved concerns about specimen export.
The journal updated its policy on fossil provenance, stating it will not accept papers about specimens suspected to be illegally collected or exported.
The permanent withdrawal rekindled Brazilian demands for repatriation, and the German ministry said it will reexamine the processes and explore an agreeable solution.
A preprint analysis found that Germany, the UK, and France contributed more than 10% of paleontology papers but most research used fossils from abroad, often without local authors.
Some paleontologists argued fossils are safer in European or US institutions, while Brazilian scientists countered that disasters can happen anywhere.
The controversy prompted voluntary repatriation of a spider fossil and 35 other specimens from the University of Kansas Natural History Museum to Brazil.
The retraction left the species Ubirajara jubatus nonexistent to science, as described by paleontologist Felipe Pinheiro.

1-14990-2-1.subevent: NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope captured enough light from exoplanets to identify molecules in their atmospheres for the first time, a significant step toward detecting possible life.
Spitzer project scientist Dr. Michael Werner expressed surprise at the achievement, saying they had no idea Spitzer would make such a dramatic step.
Spitzer obtained spectra for two gas exoplanets, HD 209458b and HD 189733b, and the data indicated they are drier and cloudier than predicted, with no water found.
Astronomers suggested water might be hidden under thick clouds, and HD 209458b showed hints of silicate dust in its atmosphere.
Dr. Jeremy Richardson, lead author of a Nature paper, stated that water must be hidden by a dusty cloud layer.
Two other teams, led by Dr. Carl Grillmair and Dr. Mark R. Swain, also captured spectra of the exoplanets and obtained similar results.
A spectrum reveals chemical fingerprints by splitting light into wavelengths; until these observations, only solar system planets had spectra available.
The exoplanets are extremely far away, with HD 189733b 370 trillion miles and HD 209458b 904 trillion miles from Earth.
Spitzer used the 'secondary eclipse' technique, measuring the dip in infrared light as planets passed behind their stars, to isolate the planets' light.
In the studies, Spitzer's spectrograph stared at the transiting planets and subtracted the star's spectrum to obtain the planets' spectra alone.
Dr. Carl Grillmair noted that the observations were considered high risk but Spitzer performed superbly.
Previous Hubble observations of HD 209458b revealed elements like sodium, with less sodium than predicted, supporting the idea of high clouds.
Astronomers hope to use Spitzer for further studies of transiting exoplanets, with at least three more candidates for obtaining spectra.

0-4469-10-1.subevent: The vast majority of economists polled by Reuters said President Donald Trump’s import tariffs will do more harm than good to the U.S. economy.
All 104 economists polled by Reuters expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates next week, with three more hikes to follow this year.
Nearly 90 percent of 71 respondents said they were concerned tariffs on steel and aluminum imports would lead to a wider trade war.
Ethan Harris, head of global economics at BofAML, expressed concern about the persistence and scope of protectionism.
Nearly 80 percent of 60 economists said the tariffs would do more harm than good, and none said they would benefit the U.S. economy.
Stefan Koopman of Rabobank warned that the tariffs are likely to be met with retaliation and could undermine global economic expansion.
The OECD raised its global growth forecasts but warned that the world economy was vulnerable to trade tensions after the import tariffs.
The U.S. dollar extended its retreat against most major currencies following Trump's tariff decision.
The Fed is expected to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at the March 20-21 meeting and repeat that move three more times this year.
The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the core PCE price index, is forecast to reach 2 percent in the third quarter.
Economic growth is forecast at an annualized rate of 2.5-3.0 percent each quarter this year.
Thirty-one of 58 economists said they were not concerned about fiscal stimulus bringing the next downturn closer, while 27 were concerned.
The median probability of a recession in the coming year was 13 percent, up from 10 percent in a November poll.

13-23825-1-t.subevent: The ASA ruled that Channel 4's Big Fat Gypsy Weddings poster campaign was irresponsible, offensive, reaffirmed negative stereotypes, and depicted a child in a sexualised way.
Channel 4's four posters promoted the second series and featured the words 'Bigger. Fatter. Gypsier' over images of Gypsy boys and girls.

Yvonne MacNamara, chief executive of the Irish Traveller Movement in Britain, said that as a result of the decision, Channel 4's brand has been held up to be morally bankrupt and called on the broadcaster to hang its head in shame.
The Irish Traveller Movement in Britain and co-complainants successfully appealed against the ASA's original decision not to investigate the campaign despite nearly 400 complaints.
The ASA found that one of the girls in a low-cut top with heavy makeup and visible bra was 15, a year below the legal age for appearing in ads.
The ASA said Channel 4 acted irresponsibly by depicting a child in a sexualised way.
The ASA also ruled that the image of an aggressive-looking young boy endorsed negative stereotypes and was likely to cause distress and mental harm to Gypsy and Traveller children.
Channel 4 said the ad campaign used real and intimate photographic portraits in a journalistic style that reflected the journalistic intent of the series.
A Channel 4 spokesman apologised for any offense caused and stated that they had taken responsible action pre-publication, including obtaining consent and submitting to the CAP copy advice team.
Channel 4 chief creative officer Jay Hunt announced that the broadcaster would not make any more series of Big Fat Gypsy Weddings but would produce six Gypsy-themed one-off specials next year.
In March, media regulator Ofcom dismissed complaints that the TV campaign breached any aspects of the broadcasting code.
David Enright, a partner at law firm Howe & Co, said the ASA's findings represent a fundamental turning point in how Travellers and Gypsies can be portrayed in the media.

0-4321-1-1.subevent: A man with a sword-like weapon and a firearm entered the Savo Vocational College inside the Herman shopping centre.
The man killed one person and wounded at least nine others at the school.
Police were forced to use a gun to stop the violence at the shopping centre.
Police did not confirm that they shot the suspect, who is a Finnish national.
Police reported that one person died and 10 people, including the suspect and a police officer, were injured, with two victims suffering serious injuries.
Prime Minister Antti Rinne tweeted that the violence was 'shocking and totally condemnable'.
Finnish media reported that the attacker allegedly entered the college with some sort of sword.

6-18793-1-t.subevent: Pope Francis breaks a 15-month hiatus from international travel with a historic visit to Iraq.
Matteo Bruni announces the news on Monday that the Pope has accepted the invitation of the Republic of Iraq and the local Catholic Church.
The Apostolic Journey will cover four days and four Iraqi provinces, including Baghdad, Ur, Erbil, Mosul, and Qaraqosh.
The itinerary will be released later, taking into consideration the evolution of the worldwide health emergency.
Pope Francis has long expressed his desire to visit Iraq, having told a meeting of Catholic aid agencies on 10 June 2019 that he planned to travel there in 2020.
The visit realizes a dream of Pope St. John Paul II, who planned to travel to Iraq at the end of 1999 but was postponed by Saddam Hussein.
Cardinal Louis Raphael Sako says Pope Francis will receive an enthusiastic welcome in Iraq, as everyone esteems him for his simplicity and nearness.
Pope Francis met Iraqi President Barham Salih on 25 January, and they spoke about preserving the historical presence of Christians in the country and ensuring their security.
Christians' presence in Iraq has drastically diminished from 1-1.4 million before 2003 to 300-400 thousand after war and IS occupation.
Iraq's president and prime minister have often invited Christians who fled to return and help rebuild the nation.
Recovery has been impeded by economic crisis, corruption, and 1.7 million internally displaced people, with UNICEF estimating 4 million Iraqis requiring assistance.
Cardinal Sako says Pope Francis' visit will bring a breath of fresh hope to the long-suffering nation.

8-6204-1-5.subevent: Authorities announce two people are dead after bushfires on Kangaroo Island, and forensic police are on the way.
Premier Steven Marshall reiterates warnings for people to listen to alerts from the CFS.
Daylight reveals devastation with a massive bushfire tearing through about 150,000 hectares of land.
The iconic Southern Ocean Lodge is totally destroyed; operators express shock and say they will rebuild.
Most emergency level fires have eased but one on the western half of the island remains uncontrolled.
Unconfirmed reports emerge of many homes and other buildings, including tourism accommodation, being destroyed.
Mayor Michael Pengilly says the destruction is immense with large losses of livestock and property.
The CFS issues an extreme fire danger warning for the Ravine fire on the western end of Kangaroo Island.
Local MP Leon Bignell says people on the island are in shock and frightened after the fire.
The CFS urges people to defer all non-essential travel to Kangaroo Island, with ferry priority given to fire vehicles.
Mayor Pengilly says part of the island looks like it has been hit by a nuclear bomb.
Mainland SA experiences smoke and dust, with health advice for those with chest conditions; Victoria and NSW brace for catastrophic conditions.

0-4480-4-t.subevent: Two years after the antisemitic attack on the synagogue in Halle, vigils and rallies took place in the city.
Saxony-Anhalt's Minister President Haseloff called for civil courage and warned against a coarsening of language.
Several hundred people paused for minutes of reflection at noon on Saturday to publicly remember the victims of the terrorist attack of October 9, 2019.
On the market square, life stood still for a moment.
In memory of the victims and survivors, actions, vigils, and rallies were planned in the city until evening.

0-4299-6-4.subevent: Ukraine's government and pro-Russia rebels agreed a memorandum on a peace plan for the eastern conflict.
The nine-point deal includes setting up a 30km buffer zone, a ban on overflights of part of eastern Ukraine by military aircraft, and the withdrawal of foreign mercenaries on both sides.
The agreement was announced at talks in the Belarusian capital Minsk.
More than 3,000 have died in fighting in two eastern regions since April.
The original ceasefire agreed on 5 September has been frequently violated but is still holding.
Ukraine accuses Russia of arming separatists and sending Russian troops to the eastern Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
The Kremlin denies it has any role there.
Three powerful blasts rocked the main rebel-held city of Donetsk, with eyewitnesses saying that a chemical plant may have been hit.
A humanitarian convoy of about 200 lorries from Russia arrived in Donetsk.
Russia says the convoy delivered food, water, and generators, but this was done without Ukraine's authorisation.
The deal was reached after late-night talks between representatives of Ukraine, Russia, eastern separatists and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Former Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, representing Kiev at the talks, said that all sides had agreed to move back some of their heavy weapons.
Kuchma said heavy artillery will be moved 15km away from the front line.
Kuchma added that the deal would be implemented within 24 hours and monitors from the OSCE would travel to the buffer zone to check for compliance.
Separatist leader Alexander Zakharchenko said that the two sides did not discuss the status of the rebel-held areas of Luhansk and Donetsk.
Earlier this week, Ukraine's parliament passed a bill granting a three-year self-rule to parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
The Russian ambassador to Ukraine, Mikhail Zurabov, said that mercenaries were fighting on both sides and called on OSCE to oversee their removal.
Russia has repeatedly said that any of its citizens fighting alongside separatists in Ukraine are doing so in a private capacity.
There are now fears in Ukraine that Russia wants to create a frozen conflict in eastern Ukraine.

1-14897-1-2.subevent: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon rose more than 50% in the first three months of 2020 compared to the same period in 2019, according to preliminary satellite data.

Scientists warned that Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro's development-friendly policies could transform the Amazon rainforest into a drier, savannah-like landscape once a 'tipping point' is crossed.
Brazil's environmental agency scaled back enforcement measures during the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving the forest and indigenous tribes more vulnerable.
Laercio Guajajara, a member of the Guajajara tribe, told ABC News that their territory is invaded by loggers and hunters, with many invasions ongoing.
Andre Karipuna, a member of the Karipuna tribe, told the Environmental Justice Foundation that the community is desperate because one infected person could spread the virus to the whole tribe.
Bolsonaro slashed funding and enforcement at FUNAI, Brazil's department of indigenous affairs, since taking office in 2019.
In July 2019, Bolsonaro appointed a federal police officer with connections to agribusiness to head FUNAI.
The Guajajara tribe's 'Guardians' conducted patrols to defend their lands, as documented by ABC News in a documentary titled 'Guardians of the Amazon'.
In April 2020, FUNAI passed law IN 09, which prevents indigenous lands awaiting official demarcation from being labelled as 'indigenous' in the land registry.
Environmental groups alleged that law IN 09 provides a route for illegal occupiers of indigenous lands to claim the land is not indigenous.

Bolsonaro's Provisional Measure 910, first decreed in December 2019, allows those who illegally deforested and occupied protected federal lands before December 2018 to purchase the property at reduced prices.
Critics alleged that MP 910 rewards illegal land grabbers, and an analysis by IMAZON found the measure could lead to added deforestation of up to 16,000 square kilometers by 2027.

The Bolsonaro administration denied that MP 910 would facilitate land-grabbing, arguing that new landowners must preserve 80% of their land and only those occupying peacefully for many years would get titles.
Since the enforcement rollbacks, reports of illegal logging and violent attacks across indigenous reserves increased.

In early April, Yanomami reserve leaders reported an increase in illegal gold mining during the pandemic, and BBC Brasil published satellite photos showing miners entering an area with an isolated community.
Some leaders blamed the invasions for the April 10 death of a 15-year-old Yanomami boy, the first known from the tribe to die from the virus.
The Karipuna tribe submitted a complaint to federal prosecutors on April 8 stating that non-indigenous people were clearing inside their reserve.
On April 18, a 33-year-old indigenous leader of the Uru-eu-wau-wau reserve was reportedly assassinated.
In March, Zezico Rodrigues Guajajara of the Guajajara tribe was killed by a shotgun-wielding assailant, becoming the fifth Guajajara murdered in five months.
Erival Guajajara, a member of the Guajajara tribe, told ABC News that they are afraid for their lives because of their vulnerability.

32-wiki-img/2081-1/2081-1-2.subevent: Washington becomes the first US state to legalize human composting.
Governor Jay Inslee signs the bill into law on Tuesday.
Katrina Spade, who lobbied for the law, founded a company called Recompose that could be the first to provide the service.
Spade says recomposition offers an alternative to embalming and burial or cremation that is natural, safe, and sustainable, with significant savings in carbon emissions and land usage.
The process involves placing a body in a hexagonal steel container filled with alfalfa, wood chips, and straw.
The container is shut and the body decomposes naturally within 30 days, creating two wheelbarrows' worth of soil.
Loved ones are given the soil, which they can use in planting flowers, vegetables, or trees.
Environmentally friendly burial alternatives are becoming increasingly popular.
Late actor Luke Perry was laid to rest in a 'mushroom suit' in California.
The suit's creator says it reduces toxic pollutants released during decomposition and cremation.

3-17461-8-t.subevent: A hacking group linked to Iran attempted to break into President Trump’s re-election campaign but was unsuccessful.
Microsoft reported significant cyber activity by the group targeting current and former U.S. officials, journalists, and prominent Iranians.
Trump campaign director Tim Murtaugh said the campaign had no indication its infrastructure was targeted.
Over a 30-day period, the group made more than 2,700 attempts to identify consumer email accounts and attacked 241, compromising four accounts not associated with the campaign.
Microsoft did not identify the targeted election campaign; 19 Democrats and three Republicans are running.
Hacking to interfere in elections has been a concern since Russia’s 2016 operation.
Tensions between the U.S. and Iran have risen since Trump withdrew from the nuclear accord and reinstated sanctions.
Iran did not immediately comment on Microsoft’s statement.
The group Phosphorous used information gathering to game password reset features and attempted to take over accounts; attacks were not technically sophisticated.
Microsoft has tracked Phosphorous since 2013 and took control of 99 websites the group used in March.
The 2016 Clinton campaign was hacked in a cyberattack on Democratic Party organizations.
Big tech companies met with U.S. intelligence agencies in September to discuss security strategies.

17-27607-1-t.subevent: The French rugby federation (FFR) voted unanimously to allow transgender women to play women's rugby as of next season.
World Rugby advised against transgender women playing women's contact rugby on safety grounds, but the advice was not binding.
Serge Simon, Vice President of FFR, said in a statement that rugby is an inclusive sport without discrimination.
The FFR clarified that transgender women must have been on hormonal treatment for at least 12 months and have testosterone below five nanomoles per liter to compete.
Transgender women who have already transitioned and changed their civil record can play without preconditions.
The FFR is the first national federation in France to allow transgender women to compete in top level sport.

0-4763-2-1.subevent: Flight JT610 lost contact with ground officials 13 minutes after takeoff on Monday and crashed into waters about 30-35 meters deep off the coast of Java.
Safety experts said the top priority of the investigation will be finding the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder.
The pilots had asked to turn back to base shortly before losing contact with air traffic control, according to an Indonesian air navigation spokesman.
Flight tracking data showed that two minutes into the flight, the plane reached 2,000 feet, then descended more than 500 feet and veered left before climbing to 5,000 feet.
In its final moments, the plane gained speed to 345 knots before data was lost at 3,650 feet.
Greg Waldron, managing editor of Flightglobal Asia, said recovering the black boxes should be easier due to the shallow water depth.
Lion Air CEO Edward Strait said the crashed jet had a technical problem on a flight from Bali to Jakarta on Sunday, but the issue was resolved according to procedure.
Lion Air's only prior fatal accident before this crash was in 2004, when an MD-82 crashed upon landing at Solo City, killing 25 people.
Six other Lion Air jets, including one that crash-landed into water at Bali in 2013, were damaged beyond repair in various accidents, according to the Aviation Safety Network.
In June 2016, the European Union removed Lion Air from its air safety blacklist.

Airbus and Boeing have waged a dispute over subsidies at the WTO since 2004, and the WTO is due to decide early next year on the level of annual tariffs the EU can impose on U.S. imports.

9-21116-1-1.subevent: Barbara Jatta says the intention is to reopen the Vatican Museums on 1 February.
Jatta says the closure has been extended for an extra 15 days beyond the previously set 16 January, in accordance with board decisions and Italian government indications.
Jatta notes the seven-kilometre itinerary for small groups does not constitute a health problem and says reopening would be a nice message.
Jatta participated in the “More Museum” conference on Thursday.
Jatta says there has been a huge increase in visitors through the website and social media, especially during strict lockdown.
Jatta highlights the success of daily Instagram posts and 'Face to Face' videos showing museum work during closure.
Jatta hopes the opportunities offered by social media will continue to be part of the museum’s life.
Jatta notes an increase in young visitors between 18 and 30 due to cheaper ticket options.
Jatta reiterates that activity never stopped; since the 6 November closure, all restorers and personnel came to work respecting rules.
Jatta says editorial work, research, restoration, construction sites, and laboratories are all running, and she focused on collections, maintenance, catalogue, research, and publications.
Jatta expresses hope that the museums will open soon, depending on Italian government decisions.

9-21087-5-t.subevent: Indiana Superintendent of Public Instruction Dr. Jennifer McCormick announced that all K-12 schools will remain closed through the end of the school year.
All K-12 schools in Indiana shall provide instruction via remote learning for the remainder of the 19-20 school year.
Schools will not conduct in-person instruction through the remainder of the school year.
The state is reviewing the amount of instructional days required for schools, and all schools previously received a 20-day waiver to reduce required days to 160.
Schools must now provide e-learning until they complete 160 instructional days or at least 20 additional days of remote learning between April 2 and the end of the school year.
If a school completes the 20 days but falls short of 160, the Indiana Department of Education will waive the difference.
Schools are required to submit a continuous learning plan by April 17.
McCormick stated the department is committed to working with schools and that the plans signal to families, students, and policymakers what instruction looks like.
McCormick said one of the department’s goals is to get graduates across the stage, providing flexibility for high school seniors on track to graduate as of March 19 to earn an Indiana diploma.
Superintendent of Indianapolis Public Schools Aleesia Johnson expressed support for the decision and said the district will continue working to serve students and families.

0-4506-1-1.subevent: Indigenous protesters paralyzed roads around Ecuador and blocked a main highway into the capital in a fifth day of action.
President Lenín Moreno eliminated fuel subsidies last week.
The umbrella indigenous organization Conaie said demonstrations would continue until President Moreno withdraws the measure.
Conaie president Jaime Vargas said more than 20,000 protesters would arrive in Quito to demand that the government overturn the decree, coinciding with a national strike.
President Moreno said he would not tolerate disorder nor overturn the fuel price hike.
Interior minister Paula Romo said detentions had risen to 477 since Thursday, mainly for vandalism.
Indigenous and workers' movements blocked roads on Monday with stones, tires, and burning branches.
The northern entry to Quito was paralyzed.
Police erected barricades around the presidential palace and closed off the downtown area while Moreno presided over a government security council meeting to assess the crisis.
The government reported that two dozen policemen were injured in clashes and a man died when he was hit by a car and an ambulance could not reach him through the barricades.
Authorities rounded up about 20 shopkeepers for raising food prices illegally due to higher fuel costs.
A state of emergency was declared.
In a national address, President Moreno reiterated calls for dialogue and said resources would be set aside to help the poor and compensate for price rises.

9-21449-4-t.subevent: The United States established diplomatic relations with Uganda in 1962 following Uganda's independence from the United Kingdom.
Uganda endured despotism and near economic collapse in the post-independence period.
Human rights abuses by several Ugandan governments strained U.S. relations with Uganda.
President Museveni came to power in 1986 after decades of internal strife.
Under Museveni, Uganda experienced relative political stability, democratic progress, and economic growth.
Uganda made strides in reducing HIV/AIDS, experienced economic growth, and stabilized its north where the Lord's Resistance Army operated.
Uganda faced numerous challenges including population growth, power and infrastructure constraints, corruption, underdeveloped democratic institutions, and human rights deficits.
Uganda became a key U.S. strategic partner particularly through its contribution to the African Union Mission in Somalia.
Uganda and other governments of the region, under the African Union and with U.S. support, weakened the Lord's Resistance Army and reduced its threat to central Africa.
The United States became Uganda's largest bilateral donor with assistance enhancing social and economic well-being.
More than 700,000 Ugandans received life-saving antiretroviral treatment funded by U.S. assistance.
In post-conflict northern Uganda, the United States shifted its support from emergency humanitarian assistance to longer-term development programs.
Since 2011, the United States provided a small number of military advisers to the LRA-affected region to enhance the capacity of regional militaries.
The United States supported efforts to bring the Lord's Resistance Army's top leaders to justice, promote defections, and assist affected communities.
Uganda became eligible for preferential trade benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act.
The United States committed to signing trade and investment framework agreements with the East African Community and the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa.
Uganda and the United States belonged to several international organizations including the United Nations, International Monetary Fund, World Bank, and World Trade Organization.
The current U.S. Ambassador to Uganda was Deborah Malac.
Uganda maintained an embassy in the United States at 5911 16th Street NW, Washington, DC.

11-23170-3-t.subevent: Facebook reached an agreement with the Australian government and will restore news pages in the country.
The Australian government introduced last-minute changes to the proposed news media bargaining code.
The bill is expected to be voted into law soon.
Facebook said it is satisfied that the Australian government agreed to changes and guarantees addressing its core concerns.
Facebook announced it will restore news on Facebook for Australians in the coming days.
The law will make digital platforms pay local media outlets and publishers for linking their content.
Under amendments, the government will consider commercial agreements digital platforms have already made before deciding if the code applies.
The government will give digital platforms one month's notice before reaching a final decision.
A two-month mediation period will allow digital platforms and publishers to broker deals before arbitration.
The arbitration clause allows government-appointed arbitrators to decide the final price, ruling in favor of either party.
The government said the amendments provide further clarity and impetus for commercial negotiations.
Seven West Media signed a letter of intent to provide news content to Facebook.
Google previously threatened to remove its search service but later struck commercial deals with local publishers.
Facebook removed news features from Australia, blocking users from viewing or sharing news.
The move faced backlash from politicians and users after government health and emergency pages were blocked.
Treasurer Josh Frydenberg contacted Facebook chief Mark Zuckerberg to resolve issues.
Facebook VP Campbell Brown said the Australian government clarified that Facebook retains the ability to decide if news appears on its platform.

26-14496-2-t.subevent: Sebastien Buemi was forced to curtail his first stint in the #8 TS050 Hybrid with a suspected puncture.
The two Toyotas initially traded the lead based on their stints, but the #7 car established a net lead through quicker pitstops.

The third-placed #1 car of Gustavo Menezes was in danger of being lapped after four hours.
The fourth-placed #3 car of Romain Dumas was lapped.

13-24524-1-1.subevent: Roman Catholic bishops voted on a summary document at the close of the controversial Catholic synod.
Pope Francis described the Vatican summit as a way to open up broader horizons, rising above conspiracy theories and blinkered viewpoints.
The final document released by the Vatican was by no means a triumph for progressives.
The document reflects the continuing deep rift between conservative and progressive factions within the church hierarchy.
The language describing same-sex marriage as 'not even remotely analogous' to heterosexual marriage marked a clear victory for the conservative camp.
The bishops concluded that there were 'absolutely no grounds' for gay marriage and that homosexuals should not be discriminated against.
Pope Francis alluded to the scandal and rumor that plagued the divisive Synod, saying opinions were expressed freely but not always in well-meaning ways.
The final ruling will come as a blow to countless LGBT Catholics who were hoping for a more inclusive outcome.
Monsignor Krzysztof Charamsa announced that he was a gay, practising Catholic priest and called for the synod to take up the plight of gays.
The Vatican fired Charamsa, claiming his decision to make such a pointed statement was 'very serious and irresponsible'.
The Pope has not lifted any of the actively homophobic and transphobic policies of his predecessors.
Proposals to 'reach out' to gay people were scrapped by the Church last year and the Church has no plans to change its stance.

0-4324-1-1.subevent: Meghan Markle and Prince Harry take legal action against the publishers of a British newspaper after it published a private letter she wrote to her estranged father.
In February, the Mail on Sunday published a handwritten note shared by Thomas Markle.
The letter accuses Thomas Markle of 'turning a blind eye to the pain' he’s causing by speaking to the media.

Prince Harry posted a statement revealing that they have initiated legal proceedings against the publication and its parent company Associated Newspapers, citing misuse of private information, infringement of copyright, and breach of the Data Protection Act 2018.

Schillings, the legal firm representing the couple, called the letter's publication 'part of a campaign by this media group to publish false and deliberately derogatory stories about her, as well as her husband.'
Prince Harry defended his wife against the 'bullying.'
Prince Harry wrote that his wife has become one of the latest victims of a British tabloid press that wages campaigns against individuals with no thought to the consequences.
Prince Harry said there is a human cost to this 'relentless propaganda,' specifically when it is knowingly false and malicious.
Prince Harry noted the positive reception of the couple's current royal tour in Africa and alluded to his mother Princess Diana’s death.
Prince Harry said the positive coverage from the same publications exposes the double standards of the press pack that has vilified her almost daily for the past nine months.
Prince Harry said though this action may not be the safe one, it is the right one, and his deepest fear is history repeating itself, referencing his mother's death.
The statement added that the couple are paying for the lawsuit privately and will donate any proceeds from damages to an anti-bullying charity.
In 2016, Prince Harry issued a statement decrying the 'wave of abuse and harassment' targeting his then-girlfriend Meghan.
In May, Prince Harry accepted damages and an apology after a photo agency violated their privacy by taking up-close images of their home.
The legal proceedings riled up frequent Meghan critic Piers Morgan, who tweeted that the complaint revealed her 'true colors.'

22-wiki-img/3685-3/3685-3-2.subevent: Marine Le Pen is riding a populist insurgency and may top the first round of France's presidential election on 23 April.
Under-30s in France are more nationalistic than the general population.
Génération Identitaire (GI) specializes in publicity stunts to reclaim French territory from migrants and has 120,000 Facebook fans.
GI leader Pierre Larti verbally confronts North African men while handing out flyers.
GI is sprouting branches across Europe, seeing the continent as a battleground between European and Islamic culture.
Jean-Yves Le Gallou's video 'Being European' has been viewed over 3.2 million times on YouTube.
Fdesouche, a news aggregator, gets about 3 million views per month, dwarfing mainstream politicians' websites.
France's online far right ('fachosphère') has seen spectacular growth over the past 10 years.
Alain Soral's website Égalité et Réconciliation has more readers than Fdesouche.
At Sciences Po, Eurosceptic students set up a club called 'Critique of European Reason' (CRE).
CRE members gathered outside the UK embassy to drink champagne and sing 'God Save the Queen' after the Brexit vote.
CRE member Kevin and others describe experiencing 'anti-white racism' in immigrant suburbs.
Journalist Alexandre Devecchio calls young people preoccupied with identity erosion the 'Zemmour generation'.
Identitarians and the Zemmour generation could help Marine Le Pen win power, though it appears unlikely.

1-15208-8-t.subevent: The Obama administration announced a major step forward in medical marijuana research regulations.
The Drug Enforcement Agency neglected to deschedule marijuana as a Schedule I drug.
The DEA promised to improve access to researchers by increasing the number of federally authorized marijuana growers.
Scientists initially applauded the move but then heard the details.
Researcher Ryan Vandrey stated that adding growers will make very little change for his research.
Vandrey explained that the problem is the regulatory hoops, not a lack of supply.
Vandrey described the Schedule I license approval process, which can take up to a year and requires stringent facility requirements.
Vandrey noted that any small change in a study requires a lengthy reevaluation from the DEA, forcing his current project on hold.
Vandrey said there is no time limit on the DEA to review research, and he calls them daily to check the status.
Vandrey called for descheduling marijuana or rewriting rules to simplify researchers' access.
Vandrey expressed concern that states have legalized marijuana without adequate data on its safety as a medical treatment.
DEA head Chuck Rosenberg stated that there are no adequate safety studies, so the agency refused to deschedule marijuana.
Lawmakers, including Sen. Brian Schatz, introduced legislation to streamline the research approval process with time limits on agency review.

3-17198-4-t.subevent: Macedonia declared a state of emergency in its border areas at the end of August.
Up to 3,000 refugees arrive in Macedonia each day, and similar numbers cross into Serbia and Hungary, most hoping to reach Germany.
Germany received almost 200,000 requests for asylum in the first seven months of 2015.
More than four in 10 applicants came from the Western Balkans, with almost 30,000 from Albania and a similar number from Kosovo.
Syria is the only country with more applicants than Kosovo and Albania.
Germany received only 8,000 asylum applications from Albania during all of 2014.
In the 1990s, conflict and forced displacement drove tens of thousands of ethnic-Albanian Kosovars to Germany.
No such emergency explains this year's mass movement from Kosovo and Albania.
Albania is now a democratic country and EU membership candidate.
Kosovo and Albania share small populations, ethnic-Albanian majority, and poor economic prospects.
The Friedrich Ebert Foundation's survey in Pristina found that almost all leaving were driven by the dire economic situation and hoping to find jobs in Germany.
The BBC spoke to young people in Mitrovica who said young Kosovars were 'like birds in a cage', faced visa restrictions, and had a youth unemployment rate of around 60%.

Similar causes are behind the exodus from Albania, complicated by the return of tens of thousands who lost jobs in Greece and Italy, and Albania's average monthly wage of €350 is seen as unacceptably low.

Neither Kosovo nor Albania have been on Germany's list of 'safe countries of origin', though that is set to change, so most asylum applications are doomed to failure but it takes almost a year before many are ordered to leave.

There were almost 20,000 asylum applications from Serbia, Macedonia, and Montenegro in the year to the end of July, mostly Roma, and despite the Decade of Roma Inclusion, many Roma have been left in vulnerable situations.
Dritan Nelaj said key indicators have deteriorated compared to 10 years ago and Roma people rely on informal income while economies are formalizing, losing their position and facing discrimination.
For many Roma, heading to Germany seems attractive, trading insecure housing for asylum centres and receiving €140 per month while claims are assessed.
Milita Sunjic said Roma people complain asylum procedures are too short; they know they won't get asylum but are safe and warm.
Unlike the exodus from Kosovo and Albania, the plight of Roma is a perennial problem.
Dritan Nelaj suggested the discrimination Roma face should make them legitimate candidates for asylum.
Milita Sunjic said as long as Roma families suffer abject poverty, they will continue to try their luck in Germany.

1-15073-3-t.subevent: Hungary offered neighboring Romania help in caring for coronavirus patients as Romania faces a surge of COVID-19 cases and a shortage of intensive care beds.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto sent a letter over the weekend offering assistance to Romania in treating COVID-19 patients.
Negotiations are underway between the Romanian and Hungarian sides on the concrete form of the assistance.
Romania is the second-least vaccinated country in the EU, with 34% of adults fully vaccinated compared to 74% across the bloc.
Romanian vaccination committee chief Valeriu Gheorghita likened the situation in Romania to Italy at the start of the pandemic.
Gheorghita said hospitals and emergency units are overwhelmed by COVID-19 patients, leaving aside other health care needs.
Romania's daily COVID-19 cases skyrocketed from about 1,000 a month ago to record highs of more than 15,000 this week.
Romania registered more than 300 deaths in a single day for the first time since the pandemic started on Wednesday.
Around 1,500 COVID-19 patients are receiving care in Romania's intensive care units, stretching the health care system to capacity.
Romanian President Klaus Iohannis called the developments a 'catastrophe' this week.
Romanian authorities suspended nonemergency medical treatments for 30 days and asked the EU for help through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism.
A hospital fire in Constanta tore through an ICU for COVID-19 patients, killing seven people, days earlier.
Szijjarto wrote in a Facebook post on Saturday that Hungary's health care system has capacity to care for patients if needed.
Romania's Health Ministry did not respond to an AP email requesting specifics on the help offered by Hungary.
Hungary, with 66% of adults fully vaccinated, experienced a recent uptick in COVID-19 indicators, reaching hospitalizations not seen since early summer.
Hungary recorded 837 new COVID-19 infection cases on Thursday, compared with 14,467 in Romania.

3-17363-6-t.subevent: France's Biomérieux gave its proprietary formula to the Canadian government for free so its national lab can try to manufacture test kits on its own.
In March, Canada passed emergency legislation that gave the government and third parties the right to produce patented goods without the patent holders’ consent.
Biomérieux did not respond to questions about similar arrangements with other governments or the revenue impact of the agreement.
Biomérieux reported a 21.5% increase in sales in the first quarter, thanks in part to demand for reagent.
The Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) described the arrangement as a temporary license that allows the government to manufacture Biomérieux products for coronavirus testing, signed at no cost.
PHAC said its manufacturing was still in development and testing, and its goal was to alleviate shortages soon.
In an email to customers in early April, Biomérieux’s Canadian unit said the move was meant to clear up testing backlogs and that it was also boosting its own production.
The chemicals in short supply, called reagents, are used to extract RNA from patient samples.
Other major suppliers of RNA extraction equipment are facing soaring demand.

Biomérieux said in its customer note that it hopes the move will allow labs to test more Canadians, reducing testing backlogs, and that the collaboration signals unprecedented solutions for unprecedented times.

Biomérieux extraction equipment was the primary system used by Ontario’s public health labs, and heavy reliance on one brand contributed to a testing slowdown in late March; the equipment is also widely used in Quebec.
PHAC said the deal is an interim solution because its facilities are not meant for long-term manufacturing.
On Thursday, Canada pledged C$1.1 billion for research and drug or vaccine manufacturing in its fight against the coronavirus.

13-wiki-img/24048-2/24048-2-2.subevent: Malaysia arrested more than 4,000 people for violating virus lockdown orders.
Malaysia entered a harsher phase of its Movement Control Order called 'harsh mode'.
Senior minister Datuk Seri Ismail Sabri Yaakob stated at a press conference that enforcement had changed from soft to stern to harsh mode.
Police set up hundreds of roadblocks and arrested thousands of people, including a man who jumped into the Strait of Malacca to avoid arrest.
Malaysia reported 3,116 total cases and 50 deaths from COVID-19 as of Friday.
Google published data showing an 81% decrease in citizen presence at retail and recreation sites in Malaysia.
Authorities arrested people for allegedly spreading misinformation online about the virus.
Journalists said they are self-censoring news about the virus to avoid government punishment.
Jason Kelley of the Electronic Frontier Foundation said human rights workers and activists are in danger when governments curtail free expression during crises.
Economists said political turmoil in Kuala Lumpur will hinder the government's fight against the coronavirus.
Mahathir Mohamad tried to consolidate power in February, causing a political crisis until the old ruling party returned in March.
The old ruling party returned to power and the government started to stabilize.
Malaysia predicted a recession this year due to the coronavirus, one of the first three economies in the region to do so.
The government announced the 'People's Economic Stimulus Package' (PRIHATIN) worth $57.3 billion.
Jason Liang and Krystal Ng of Wong & Partners said the size of the stimulus package signals the government's seriousness.

0-4553-8-1.subevent: A new analysis reports that ocean temperatures are rising 40 percent faster on average than previously thought.
The U.S. government shutdown remained a logjam.
Norway disclosed the kidnapping of a tycoon’s wife.
An earlier version of the briefing misidentified the home state of a farmer who supports President Trump, stating he was from Missouri instead of Mississippi.

1-15677-2-1.subevent: The Portuguese Episcopal Conference announced on Jan. 21 that public Masses would be suspended from Jan. 23 due to the 'extreme gravity' of the coronavirus crisis.
The bishops stated that it is a moral imperative for all citizens to take maximum sanitary precautions to avoid contagion.
Portugal is experiencing a surge in COVID-19 deaths, with 609,000 cases and 9,920 deaths as of Jan. 22.
This is the second time the bishops have suspended public worship; the first was in March 2020.
The bishops said that public Masses, catechesis, and other pastoral activities requiring gatherings would be suspended from Jan. 23.
The bishops called on priests to offer livestreamed Masses.
The bishops had earlier in January called for the suspension or postponement of baptisms, confirmations, and marriages.
The bishops stated that funerals could be celebrated according to norms issued in May 2020, requiring social distancing.
A Lenten retreat for the bishops scheduled for Feb. 22-26 has been canceled.
The Shrine of Our Lady of Fatima will broadcast three Masses and two rosary prayers daily while public Masses are suspended.
The shrine's broadcast times are 11 a.m., 12:30 p.m., and 3 p.m. for Masses, and 6:30 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. for rosary.
Shrine rector Fr. Carlos Cabecinhas said that it is not the same to be physically present but that is the only way to participate now.

12-7589-1-t.subevent: On December 19, 2019, the first Interoperable Radio System (IORS) flight unit was transferred to NASA Johnson Space Center for launch on SpaceX CRS-20.
NASA Safety approved the launch of the IORS on SpaceX CRS-20 and its stowage on the International Space Station.
The IORS will support easier radio mode transitions and enable new capabilities including a higher power radio, enhanced voice repeater, updated APRS, and SSTV.
The first IORS flight unit will be installed in the ISS Columbus module.
A second IORS flight unit is expected to be launched in 2020 for installation in the Russian Service module.
A total of four flight units and ten total units will be built by the ARISS hardware team.
Future upgrades and enhancements, such as a repaired Ham Video system and L-band repeater, are in various stages of design and development.
ARISS must complete 92 engineering requirements and a Phase III safety review before the IORS can be unstowed and turned on.

20-11296-3-t.subevent: Ebook Central is introduced as an all-in-one ebook platform for research, teaching, learning, and library administration.
The research process is described as complex, and Ebook Central aims to reduce the burden of switching between platforms.
Libraries turn to Ebook Central for their ebook needs.
Ebook Central brings content from virtually every publisher into one unified experience.
Students and faculty can quickly learn the platform and easily discover and use ebook content.
Simple administration makes Ebook Central ideal for librarians.
Its easy-to-use administrative module helps libraries manage their entire acquisition program and gather actionable data.

1-16512-7-t.subevent: Marriage equality was first proposed by the Executive Yuan in 2003 but stalled due to opposition.
Legislator Yu Mei-Nu attempted to revive the proposal in 2012 but faced push-back at the committee level.
The Democratic Progressive Party came to majority power in May 2016 when Tsai Ing-wen was sworn in as president.
Tsai Ing-wen voiced her support for marriage equality in a Pride video last year, stating, 'I support marriage equality.'
Yu Mei-Nu announced plans to reintroduce marriage equality to the legislative branch later that year.
Yu Mei-Nu predicted that the legislation would not pass until the end of Tsai's term in 2020.
Jason Hsu, a member of the Kuomintang, agreed that LGBT equality is a top priority and requires cross-party collaboration.
The legislation would also allow same-sex couples to inherit wealth and property and access surrogacy arrangements.
If passed, Taiwan would become the first state in Asia to have full marriage equality.

6-19465-1-t.subevent: CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Technology (IICT) tied up with Cipla to work on anti-COVID-19 drugs.
Research on anti-viral drugs has been ongoing worldwide.
Many companies developed molecules with anti-viral properties but did not widely market them due to lack of demand.
CSIR-IICT decided to work on three molecules: remdesivir, favipiravir, and baloxavir.
Cipla urged IICT director S. Chandrasekhar to start work on these molecules immediately.
Cipla will upscale the process based on know-how from CSIR-IICT.

9-wiki-img/20371-3/20371-3-1.subevent: The Dakota County Attorney's Office announced that three Minneapolis police officers were legally justified in fatally shooting Dolal Idd.
Dakota County Attorney Kathy Keena said Idd disobeyed police orders and fired at officers first.
The decision means officers Paul Huynh, Darcy Klund and Jason Schmitt will not be charged.
Idd's father Bayle Gelle and activists held a news conference demanding Governor Tim Walz assign the case to Attorney General Keith Ellison for a second review.
Gelle said 'We will never stop this revolution — fighting for justice — and I will continue until my last breath.'
About three dozen supporters watched as speakers said Black men and people of color are disproportionately denied justice when killed by police.
Jaylani Hussein said Idd's family asked the governor's office early to refer the case to the attorney general, and that Walz failed to step in.
The governor's office declined to address the criticism; spokeswoman Claire Lancaster said the attorney general has not asked for the case.

The passenger told investigators Idd said he didn't want to go to jail and fired a gun through his window.
Minneapolis police released body camera footage that appeared to show Idd firing at police, but activists said the 27-second clip was insufficient.

11-23362-12-t.subevent: The University of Akron announced that it will discontinue three intercollegiate athletics programs at the end of the 2019-20 academic year as part of a plan to reduce the University's financial support to the Athletics Department by approximately $4.4 million.
The action is being taken as part of the University's overall redesign to emerge from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The affected sports are men's cross country, men's golf, and women's tennis.
With the change, UA, which previously sponsored 20 sports, will now have 17 sports (7 men's sports and 10 women's sports).
Akron will remain a member of The Mid-American Conference (MAC).
The move affects 23 male and 9 female student-athletes.
The elimination of these sports, along with salary reductions for select coaches, staff position eliminations, scholarship and operating expenditure reductions, will total approximately $4.4 million.
Director of Athletics Larry Williams said, "These decisions are very difficult but they are important and necessary at this time."
Williams said this action aligns UA with its Mid-American Conference peers in the total number of sports and is part of the ongoing effort to redesign the University.
Williams said he met via video conference with the affected student-athletes and committed to offering them full support if they choose to leave Akron to continue their sport at another university.

Williams said the announcement was made today to allow the student-athletes as much time as possible to find new schools and to allow the three coaches and one graduate assistant impacted time to find new positions.

In reaching the decision, the University considered factors including program cost, athletics facilities, University and community impacts, and likelihood of noteworthy success at current and future funding levels.
Further details regarding the decision can be found in the FAQ document posted on the University website.

2-35071-13-1.subevent: Over 700 Belarusians have been given refuge in Poland amid unrest and repression following August's presidential election.
Poland has given strong backing to the Belarusian democratic opposition, whose exiled leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya made a second visit to Warsaw to discuss further forms of support.
Between 18 August and 18 October, 707 Belarusians came to Poland under various forms of protection, deputy interior minister Bartosz Grodecki told the Polish Press Agency.
399 Belarusians received humanitarian visas, which are free and allow for an initial one-year stay, through a simplified and expedited procedure.
170 Belarusians were confirmed as applicants for international protection in Poland, while a further 74 declared they made the application.
119 Belarusians came with visas for entrepreneurs granted as part of the "Poland. Business Harbour" programme.
64 Belarusians were allowed to enter Poland on a case-by-case basis decided by the headquarters of the Border Guard.

1-14830-1-1.subevent: New UC Riverside research finds that Venus might not be a waterless hellscape if Jupiter hadn't altered its orbit.

If tipping points are more likely, the 'optimal policy' aligns with limiting warming to 1.5°C, requiring an emergency response.
The Amundsen Sea embayment of West Antarctica might have passed a tipping point, with the 'grounding line' retreating irreversibly.
A model study shows that collapse of the Amundsen Sea embayment could destabilize the rest of the West Antarctic ice sheet, leading to about 3 metres of sea-level rise over centuries to millennia.
Palaeo-evidence shows that widespread collapse of the West Antarctic ice sheet has occurred repeatedly in the past.
Part of the East Antarctic ice sheet, the Wilkes Basin, might be similarly unstable and could add another 3–4 metres to sea level on timescales beyond a century.
The Greenland ice sheet is melting at an accelerating rate and could add a further 7 metres to sea level over thousands of years if it passes a threshold.
Models suggest that the Greenland ice sheet could be doomed at 1.5°C of warming, which could happen as soon as 2030.
We might already have committed future generations to living with sea-level rises of around 10 metres over thousands of years.
Other tipping points could be triggered at low levels of global warming, including a cluster of abrupt shifts between 1.5°C and 2°C involving sea ice.
Ocean heatwaves have led to mass coral bleaching and loss of half of the shallow-water corals on Australia's Great Barrier Reef.
A staggering 99% of tropical corals are projected to be lost if global average temperature rises by 2°C.
Biosphere tipping points can trigger abrupt carbon release back to the atmosphere, amplifying climate change.
Deforestation and climate change are destabilizing the Amazon rainforest, with estimates of a tipping point ranging from 40% deforestation to just 20% forest-cover loss.
About 17% of the Amazon has been lost since 1970.
Tipping points could interact to produce cascading effects, potentially leading to a 'hothouse' Earth.
Some scientists counter that the possibility of global tipping remains highly speculative.
The article argues that given its huge impact and irreversible nature, any serious risk assessment must consider the evidence for global tipping.
If damaging tipping cascades can occur and a global tipping point cannot be ruled out, this is an existential threat to civilization.
The evidence from tipping points alone suggests that we are in a state of planetary emergency.

4-35937-6-2.subevent: Internal conflict in Ethiopia has driven more than 50,000 refugees into Sudan in just over a month.

0-4348-1-1.subevent: Rohan Ramchandani sues Citigroup for more than $112 million, alleging it made false statements to U.S. prosecutors that led to his trial on forex-rigging charges.

1-14865-1-1.subevent: NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope captured enough light from exoplanets to identify molecules in their atmospheres for the first time.

Astronomers hope to obtain spectra for smaller, rocky exoplanets to look for signs of life.
Spitzer used the 'secondary eclipse' technique to separate the planet's light from its star's light.
Previous Hubble observations of HD 209458b revealed individual elements and supported the idea of high clouds.
